While the face was on screen, participants were asked to rate "How emotionally intense is this facial expression?"
Participants had an unlimited time to rate the faces.

Individual participants were excluded when they produced incomplete datasets (Experiment 1a, N = 3; Experiment 1b, N = 1), took part in the experiment a second time (second attempt excluded; Experiment 1a, N = 1; Experiment 1b N = 3), had fewer than 90 valid trials after individual trial exclusions (N = 0), or identified less than 70% of the audio statements correctly in the catch trials (Experiment 1a, N = 6; Experiment 1b, N = 9).
In Experiment 1a, one additional participant was excluded and in Experiment 1b, 14 additional participants were excluded.

Twenty-seven catch trials were included in the task to check that participants were paying attention to the audio (see Experiments 1a and 1b), with at least 4 per block, and at least 2 additional catch trials were included in the practice block.

Participants were excluded when they had incomplete datasets due to technical issues (Experiment 2b, N = 1), took part a second time (second attempt excluded; Experiment 2b, N = 1), had less than 90 trials after trial exclusions (N = 1, Experiment 2b), or did not identify 70% of the audio correctly in the catch trials (N = 10, Experiment 2a; N = 18, Experiment 2b).

Before the initial face changed expression, participants were presented with two possible written news statements that could evoke happiness or sadness, one of which they could decide to "give" to the other person.
One hundred and twenty-five participants, with normal or corrected-to-normal vision, recruited through Prolific, took part in a preregistered online study.
Participants recruited through Prolific were aged 18 to 30 years, resided in the UK or Ireland, and their first language was English.
After exclusions (see Exclusion Criteria), 93 participants were included (18 to 30 years, Mage = 24.59, SDage = 3.7; 45 males, 1 non-binary; 10 left-handed, 4 ambidextrous).
Participants provided informed consent prior to participating in the study.
Due to online data collection, we recruited two more participants for look 2 than intended (93 instead of 91) and adjusted the design parameters accordingly.

Ten happy statements and ten sad statements, which were rated as the most emotionally intense in a separate experiment (participants were asked, "What intensity of emotion would this news evoke if it was given to a person?"
The experiment was set up so that participants gave an equal number of happy and sad news over its course (108 each).
Participants completed 10 practice trials and 216 experimental trials across six blocks.
Blocks were separated by a 30s break, which participants were able to extend as needed.

Catch trials looked like a regular trial where participants gave news, however, after choosing the news, participants were presented with the chosen statement and a corresponding "incorrect" statement and had to select which one they had chosen (e.g., "I got a call from your mom.
Positions of these statements were randomized and no feedback was provided.

Twenty-four other participants were excluded due to a low correlation between the average proportion of "different" responses across probe distances for happy and sad facial expressions and no participants were excluded due to a large proportion of different responses for incongruent compared to congruent presentations.
Here, participants were never asked to judge the emotion in the expression, merely to perceptually compare whether one expression was identical to a probe face presented after.

Participants (Experiment 2a, N = 122; Experiment 2b, N = 148) were recruited through the Psychology Research Participation Scheme at the University of Aberdeen (Experiment 2a, N = 83; Experiment 2b, N = 138) and/or through Testable Minds (Experiment 2a, N = 39; Experiment 2b, N = 10).
Participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and hearing.

After exclusions (see Exclusion Criteria), 100 participants took part in Experiment 2a (18 to 49 years, Mage = 26.17, SDage = 9.4; 31 males, 2 did not indicate their sex; 11 left-handed, 2 ambidextrous) and 100 participants in Experiment 2b (18 to 44 years, Mage = 22.14, SDage = 5.84; 17 males, 1 did not indicate their sex; 5 left-handed).
Participants provided informed consent prior to participating in the study.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Participants provided informed consent prior to participating in the study. The study was approved by the School of Psychology ethics board of the University of Aberdeen. This experiment used preregistered sequential analyses (Lakens, 2014 (Lakens,, 2022)). Power analysis was based on the effect size of the crucial Face Emotion and News Statement interaction in Supplementary Experiment 2 (one-sided padjusted = .058, d = .15), which employed a similar experimental paradigm as in Experiment 3. As we aimed to increase the effect size by adapting the experimental paradigm of Supplementary Experiment 2 (see Stimulus and Apparatus, Procedure), we targeted an effect size of d = .2. Given a one-sided test with alpha of .05, power of 80%, four looks, and the O'Brien-Fleming type alpha and beta spending functions, maximally 181 participants would be needed, after exclusions. The four preregistered looks were at 40% (N = 73), 50% (N = 91), 75% (N = 136), and 100% of the data (N = 181). Alpha boundaries for these looks were p = .002 (look 1), p = .005 (look 2), p = .022 (look 3), and p = .043 (look 4), allowing to stop data collection early when the p-value is smaller than the boundary. Beta boundaries were p = .511 (look 1), p = .374 (look 2), and p = .129 (look 3), allowing to stop for futility when the p-value is larger than these boundaries. Due to online data collection, we recruited two more participants for look 2 than intended (93 instead of 91) and adjusted the design parameters accordingly. Data collection was stopped at this look.

A typical finding in motion perception tasks like ours is that people generally overestimate motion they observe, identifying more pronounced frames as the last seen image in the motion sequence than was really shown, across stimulus domains (e.g., facial expressions, Yoshikawa & Sato, 2008; Prigent et al., 2018; but see Thornton, 2014); abstract stimuli, Freyd & Finke, 1984; for a review, see Hubbard, 2005; actions, Currie et al., 2025; Hudson, Nicholson, Ellis, & Bach, 2016; Hudson, Nicholson, Simpson et al., 2016). These biases are taken as evidence for the predictive nature of motion perception, where expectations about a motion's next steps become integrated with its perceptual representation (Hogendoorn, 2022; White, 2026). Experiments 2a and 2b test for the first time whether, in face emotion perception, these overestimations are shaped by participants' prior expectations about the person's emotional state. If so, then participants should not only identify more expressive probe faces as identical to the last seen expression, but these overestimations should increase when the facial expressions (e.g., a smile) were expected from the prior emotion statement (e.g., "I feel so happy!" ; congruent) than when it was not expected ("I feel so sad!" ; incongruent). Such findings would provide the first evidence that prior information does not only change how people rate emotional expressions (as in Experiments 1a and 1b) but also how they perceptually represent them. Across experiments, we varied the duration between the final frame of the morph sequence and the onset of the probe (Experiment 2a, 1000 ms; Experiment 2b, 333 ms). Studies outside of emotion perception suggest that the largest predictive influences on motion perception are at about 300 ms after stimulus presentation (e.g., Hubbard, 2005; Zucchini et al., 2023). However, these timings usually reflect influences of lower-order expectations derived directly from the seen motion itself (e.g., a simple extrapolation of prior trajectories). A recent study suggests that integration of higher-order expectations and sensory information happens at a later stage, when recurrent processing between levels in the hierarchy has taken place (Ntikas et al., 2025, also see Hogendoorn, 2022). Therefore, varying the timing between to-be-judged stimulus and reference image allows us to test whether any predictive influence on emotion perception is immediate, or occurs only after recurrent feedback processes were able to affect the representation of the seen stimulus. The sample size was partly determined by a pilot study (unpublished) using a probe response task, which yielded an effect size of ηp² = .08 (Cohen's d = .29) for the crucial Face Emotion and Emotion Statement interaction (65 participants after exclusions). We aimed for a larger number of participants (N = 100) to allow for smaller effect sizes to be found. Sensitivity analysis, using G*Power 3.1.9.6 (Faul et al., 2009), showed that 100 participants allow us to detect an effect size of at least d = .28 (ηp² = .075), with .80 power and an alpha value of .05.

Experiments 2a and 2b test for the first time whether, in face emotion perception, these overestimations are shaped by participants' prior expectations about the person's emotional state. If so, then participants should not only identify more expressive probe faces as identical to the last seen expression, but these overestimations should increase when the facial expressions (e.g., a smile) were expected from the prior emotion statement (e.g., \"I feel so happy!\" ; congruent) than when it was not expected (\"I feel so sad!\" ; incongruent). Such findings would provide the first evidence that prior information does not only change how people rate emotional expressions (as in Experiments 1a and 1b) but also how they perceptually represent them. Across experiments, we varied the duration between the final frame of the morph sequence and the onset of the probe (Experiment 2a, 1000 ms; Experiment 2b, 333 ms). Studies outside of emotion perception suggest that the largest predictive influences on motion perception are at about 300 ms after stimulus presentation (e.g., Hubbard, 2005; Zucchini et al., 2023). However, these timings usually reflect influences of lower-order expectations derived directly from the seen motion itself (e.g., a simple extrapolation of prior trajectories). A recent study suggests that integration of higher-order expectations and sensory information happens at a later stage, when recurrent processing between levels in the hierarchy has taken place (Ntikas et al., 2025, also see Hogendoorn, 2022). Therefore, varying the timing between to-be-judged stimulus and reference image allows us to test whether any predictive influence on emotion perception is immediate, or occurs only after recurrent feedback processes were able to affect the representation of the seen stimulus. table.title: Overestimation of faces 1000ms give news seq replication 12_06_26
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
This study is a replication of a previous experiment that we conducted, where participants gave news (happy, sad) to a person on a screen, watched their face change expression, and compared the final expression to a probe stimulus presented shortly after. This probe stimulus was a more or less pronounced expression than the final face in the morph (-5, -3, -1, +1, +3, +5). 

If people use the news statements to predict how a person will react, then they should overestimate facial expressions to a greater extent when the news (e.g., "Hey! It seems you got the job!") is congruent with the emotion change (e.g., face changing towards a happy expression) compared to when it is incongruent.
table.design_dependent_variables:
Participants indicated whether a more expressive (forwards probe; e.g., +3) or less expressive probe (backwards probe; e.g., -3) is "same" or "different" from the last face in the face sequence.

The amount of overestimation is calculated by subtracting the proportion of "different" responses for the more expressive probes from the proportion of "different" responses for the less expressive probes, for each condition (Happy Face Happy Statement, Happy Face Sad Statement, Sad Face Happy Statement, Sad Face Sad Statement). The average for incongruent conditions is then subtracted from the average of congruent conditions. Positive values of this difference indicates greater overestimation of emotional expressions when they are congruent with the statement.
table.study_design_overview: Within-subjects design with 4 conditions: 2 Face Emotion (happy, sad) x 2 Statement Emotion (happy, sad).
table.statistical_tests:
Hypothesis: Congruent Face and Statement presentations will lead to greater overestimation compared to incongruent conditions.

We will use a one sample t-test to test whether the difference between congruent and incongruent conditions (overestimation of congruent minus overestimation for incongruent) is significantly different from zero. This is equivalent to the interaction contrast in a 2x2 ANOVA with the factors Face Emotion (happy, sad) and Statement Emotion (happy, sad).
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Participants who did not complete the full experiment or used a mobile device will be excluded. If a participant completed the experiment in multiple attempts, only the first complete attempt will be included.

Catch trials will ask participants to report which statement they just picked. Participants who did not correctly identify 60% of the statements across the experiment will be excluded.

Participants will be excluded if their correlation between "different" responses (i.e., judgement that the probe is different from the final frame of the face sequence) and the probe distance (-+1 probe, -+3 probe, -+5 probe) is smaller than 0.6. In essence, this identifies participants who are insensitive to the differences between probes that closely resemble the last seen facial expression and probes that differ more substantially.

Participants will be excluded if the absolute difference between incongruent and congruent conditions is above .3. This difference is calculated by subtracting the average proportion of "different" responses across all probes for congruent Face and Emotion Cue conditions from the proportion of "different" responses across all probes for incongruent Face and Emotion Cue conditions.

Individual trials will be excluded if the statement was picked faster than 500ms and if the response was faster than 200ms and slower than 3000ms. Participants whose final number of trials after exclusions is fewer than 90 will be excluded.
table.sample_size:
We will use sequential analyses to perform interim analyses on the data, which may allow to terminate data collection early if the effect is present when tested against a corrected alpha level or stop data collection if it is unlikely that there will be a statistically significant outcome (i.e., stop for futility).

We ran a power analysis with d = .2 for a 1-sided test with an alpha of .05, desired statistical power of 80% and four looks with the O'Brien-Fleming type alpha spending function and O'Brien-Fleming type beta spending function. This suggests that we would need 181 participants for the final look, after exclusions. We will aim to perform analyses at 40% of the data (N = 73), 50% of the data (N = 91), 75% (N = 136), and 100% of the data (N = 181). Based on the O'Brien-Fleming type alpha spending function and these four looks, the alpha boundary for the 1st look is p = .002 (z = 2.887), 2nd look is p = .005 (z = 2.577), 3rd look is p = .022 (z = 2.018), and final look is p = .043 (z = 1.721). Based on the O'Brien-Fleming type beta spending function, the beta boundary for the 1st look is .511 (z = -.028), 2nd look is .374 (z =.320), 3rd look is .129 (z = 1.129).

We will exclude participants throughout the experiment, however, will only perform statistical tests at these prespecified looks (e.g., at N = 73 after exclusions). The O'Brien-Fleming type alpha and beta spending function allows us to be flexible with data collection. In the case where we might collect more participants than planned for the 1st and 2nd look (e.g., 75 participants instead of 73), these spending functions will allow us to adjust the alpha/beta boundaries accordingly. If we collect slightly more participants than planned in the final look, we will use a user-defined spending function to adjust the alpha level at the final look.
table.additional_comments: We will also test whether facial expressions are generally overestimated by running a one-sample t-test with the average overestimation across all conditions.

Here, participants were never asked to judge the emotion in the expression, merely to perceptually compare whether one expression was identical to a probe face presented after.

text.text: Context is known to change how people evaluate facial expressions.
However, predictive processing accounts claim that context should also shape face perceptual representation, causing objectively identical expressions to appear different perceptually.

We tested this in five experiments with English-speaking adults in the UK and Ireland, recruited through a university participant pool and online platforms (total N = 413; 18-49 years; data collected 2023-2026).
Participants heard how a person was feeling, watched that person's ambiguous expression change towards a congruent or incongruent emotion, and judged the expression's final seen emotional state.
Expressions were rated as happier after happy statements and sadder after sad statements (Experiment 1a), replicating prior work.
However, they were also rated as more intense when congruent with prior statements than when incongruent (Experiment 1b), ruling out biases from statement-to-response mappings.
When participants perceptually compared final expressions with slightly more or less expressive probe faces, they generally overestimated face expressiveness (Experiments 2a, 2b).
Crucially, this overestimation was larger for expressions congruent with prior expectations, but only when the probe appeared after a longer delay (1000 vs 333 ms).
The same pattern emerged when the emotion was not explicitly stated but inferred from a variety of news that participants delivered to the person (Experiment 3).
Prior knowledge of another's emotional state therefore shapes not only the evaluation of the person's facial expressions but also their perceptual representation, consistent with predictive accounts.
Generalization to naturalistic expressions, other emotions, and cultures remains to be tested.
When meeting people, it often feels like we can just effortlessly "read" their emotions from their faces.

The ability to identify other people's emotions is crucial for smooth social interactions, and is linked to quality of life (e.g., Fulford et al., 2014), empathy (e.g., Besel & Yuille, 2010), and accuracy in judging the personality of other people (e.g., Jaksic & Schlegel, 2020).

text.text: Yet, despite the importance of emotion understanding for everyday social cognition, the mechanisms that underpin people's understanding of others' facial expressions are unclear.

Dominant proposals (e.g., basic emotion theory; Ekman & Cordaro, 2011; Izard, 2011; Levenson, 2011; Panksepp & Watt, 2011; for an overview, see Tracy & Randles, 2011) have long conceptualized emotion perception as a primarily stimulus-driven bottom-up process.

text.text: These accounts rest on the assumption that there are basic emotions (e.g., anger, fear, surprise, sadness, disgust, and happiness) that people universally experience, and that these emotions are expressed through distinct (innate) facial muscle configurations and other bodily signals.
If so, perceivers could simply "read out" the emotion in another's face by identifying (even subtle) emotion-specific facial signals.

Consistent with such views, the proposed basic emotions are recognized from their facial displays across different cultures (e.g., Ekman & Heider, 1988; for meta-analysis, see Elfenbein & Ambady, 2002), and distinct facial muscles seem to drive the recognition of certain emotions (e.g., mouth region for happiness recognition; Beaudry et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2005).

Research has indicated that the emotions people experience in daily life are rarely accompanied by the proposed stereotypical emotion displays, and that typical emotion displays are much more ambiguous than assumed by basic emotion theories (Barrett et al., 2019; Durán & Fernández-Dols, 2021).

text.text: Building on general predictive frameworks for perception and action (e.g., Bach & Schenke, 2017; Clark, 2013; Hohwy, 2013; Otten et al., 2017), these approaches assume that observers use prior information to form an internal model of another's emotional state (e.g., "She is happy"), with associated top-down predictions about how their facial expression will evolve if this internal model were correct (e.g., pulled lip corners, raised cheeks).

text.text: By testing these predictions against the sensory input, the internal model can be confirmed, and ambiguities in the sensory signals can be "filled in" by prior assumptions (e.g., Roelfsema & de Lange, 2016), so that even ambiguous expressions acquire coherent meaning.

text.text: In contrast, apparent mismatches (e.g., raised inner eyebrows and depressed lip corners associated with sadness) elicit prediction-error signals that are fed upwards along the hierarchy, triggering revisions of one's prior assumptions until sensory input and prior assumptions align (e.g., "She's not happy after all").

text.text: The hypothesis that prior information affects both how people interpret and perceptually represent emotion expressions has not been previously tested.

Prior research has investigated whether prior information is combined with information from the face when people are asked to explicitly reason about the emotion that another person experiences (e.g., Goel et al., 2024; Ong et al., 2015).

text.text: These studies do not address whether prior information changes how people represent the facial expression itself.

Other research did investigate whether contextual information affects which emotions people derive from a face (e.g., Aviezer et al., 2012; Carroll & Russell, 1996; de Gelder & Vroomen, 2000; for review and metaanalysis, see Steward et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Other research did investigate whether contextual information affects which emotions people derive from a face (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Aviezer et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Carroll & Russell, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">de Gelder & Vroomen, 2000</ref>; for review and metaanalysis, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Steward et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, these studies only asked people to evaluate the apparent emotions they recognize in a face (e.g., categorize emotion, rate emotion valence), without testing whether the perceptual representation of the face itself has changed.

Indeed, virtually none of these studies rule out simple response biases (Firestone & Scholl, 2016), where people's face emotion judgements might reflect the evaluation of the contextual information itself, instead of perceived changes in the expression (e.g., rating a face as happier not because the face appears happier but because the context is happier).

text.text: The existing research therefore says nothing about whether prior information about others affects how their facial expressions are perceptually represented.

Across five experiments, we systematically test for the first time whether prior information shapes not only how people evaluate emotional expressions they see in others, but also how they perceptually represent them.
We use the following research strategy.

Experiments 1a and 1b first establish a novel task to confirm whether simple prior information about someone's emotional state (e.g., are they happy or sad) affects emotion ratings of their facial expressions, like in prior research.

We also test whether this holds even when response biases are ruled out, by asking participants not to rate emotions themselves but instead to rate the intensity of facial expressions (irrespective of the emotion shown).

Experiments 2a and 2b then translate this design into a psychophysical task, where participants perceptually compare the last seen facial expression with a (more or less expressive) "probe" expression presented afterwards, to test whether -and under what circumstances -prior information does not only affect ratings of emotional facial expressions, but their perceptual representation itself.
Finally, the preregistered Experiment 3 extends this design into a task that more closely mirrors faceto-face interactions.

Here, participants derived expectations about others' emotional state not from experimentally given information, but from a wide variety of emotionally relevant news that they decide to give to the other person themselves.
We show that prior information shapes emotional expression's representation in this more complex ecological task, just as it does in simpler designs.
Experiments 1a and 1b developed a novel task to test whether prior information about another's emotional state affects the evaluation of their facial expressions.
In each trial, participants saw a person's face and heard how they were feeling (e.g., "I feel so happy!"
vs "I feel so sad!").
The face then either morphed towards a congruent (in 2/3 of trials) or incongruent facial expression (1/3 of trials), before disappearing at different stages mid-movement.

If prior information shapes face emotion perception, emotion ratings should not only reflect the objective amount of happiness and sadness in the facial expression (i.e., how much it has progressed through the motion sequence), but also prior information about the person's emotional state.
Happy expressions should therefore appear happier when expecting a happy compared to a sad emotional state, and vice versa for sad expressions.

In Experiment 1a, participants rated the emotion of the last seen expression in terms of given emotion labels (i.e., how happy/sad the facial expression was), like in prior research (see Steward et al., 2025).

text.text: A problem is that the ratings made from pre-given emotion labels are susceptible to response bias (e.g., Firestone & Scholl, 2016; Russell, 1993), making it unclear whether the emotional context truly affects the perception of the facial expression or only the response that participants gave.
text.formatted: A problem is that the ratings made from pre-given emotion labels are susceptible to response bias (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Firestone & Scholl, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Russell, 1993)</ref>, making it unclear whether the emotional context truly affects the perception of the facial expression or only the response that participants gave.

text.text: Here, and in prior research, higher "happy" ratings might therefore be given not because the expression truly seems happier, but because the context itself drove the higher happiness ratings, without affecting emotion perception per se.

Indeed, it is well known that pre-given emotion labels can inflate emotion recognition (Barrett et al., 2019; Nelson & Russell, 2013; Russell, 1994) and that available labels can bias ratings of identical facial expressions (Russell, 1993).
text.formatted: Indeed, it is well known that pre-given emotion labels can inflate emotion recognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Barrett et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Nelson & Russell, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Russell, 1994)</ref> and that available labels can bias ratings of identical facial expressions <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Russell, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Experiment 1b therefore did not ask participants to rate how happy/sad the last seen expression was, but to merely rate the intensity of the emotion in the expression, irrespective of which emotion was shown.
This eliminates the direct mapping between emotion ratings and context and directly measures perceived emotional intensity of the emotional expression.

If prior information shapes emotion evaluation, then we should again find that intensity ratings increase the more the expressions have progressed, and that congruent statement-face pairings are rated as more intense than incongruent ones.

or "I feel so sad!"

text.text: Experiments 1a and 1b showed that prior information about another's emotional state shapes how their facial expression is evaluated.

Importantly, this was found not only with emotion judgements, as used in prior research (Steward et al., 2025), but also with intensity judgments that eliminated the direct mapping between statement emotion and emotion rating.
text.formatted: Importantly, this was found not only with emotion judgements, as used in prior research <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Steward et al., 2025)</ref>, but also with intensity judgments that eliminated the direct mapping between statement emotion and emotion rating.

text.text: The results, therefore, provide first evidence that prior information about how a person is feeling affects how their facial expression is represented, while ruling out response biases arising from an overlap between context and the rating scale.

However, they leave open whether prior information only affects the higher-order evaluation of facial expressions, or whether it shapes the perceptual representation of the facial expression itself, in other words, whether the same face "appears" differently with different prior information.

Experiments 2a and 2b used a psychophysical task to directly test whether prior information affects the perceptual representation of observed expressions, as predicted by the tight coupling of higher-order stimulus inferences and their perceptual representation in predictive processing frameworks (e.g., Clark, 2013).

text.text: As before, people received prior (auditory) information about how a person was feeling, before watching their face change towards a congruent or incongruent expression.

Now, after the face disappeared, participants did not rate the last seen expression; instead, they compared it to a probe face image that showed the same face with a slightly more or less expressive expression (e.g., further or not as far in the morph sequence).
They pressed a button if they perceived both faces as identical and another button if they appeared different.

A typical finding in motion perception tasks like ours is that people generally overestimate motion they observe, identifying more pronounced frames as the last seen image in the motion sequence than was really shown, across stimulus domains (e.g., facial expressions, Yoshikawa & Sato, 2008; Prigent et al., 2018; but see Thornton, 2014); abstract stimuli, Freyd & Finke, 1984; for a review, see Hubbard, 2005; actions, Currie et al., 2025; Hudson, Nicholson, Ellis, & Bach, 2016; Hudson, Nicholson, Simpson et al., 2016).

text.text: These biases are taken as evidence for the predictive nature of motion perception, where expectations about a motion's next steps become integrated with its perceptual representation (Hogendoorn, 2022; White, 2026).

text.text: Experiments 2a and 2b test for the first time whether, in face emotion perception, these overestimations are shaped by participants' prior expectations about the person's emotional state.

If so, then participants should not only identify more expressive probe faces as identical to the last seen expression, but these overestimations should increase when the facial expressions (e.g., a smile) were expected from the prior emotion statement (e.g., "I feel so happy!"
; congruent) than when it was not expected ("I feel so sad!"
; incongruent).

Such findings would provide the first evidence that prior information does not only change how people rate emotional expressions (as in Experiments 1a and 1b) but also how they perceptually represent them.
Across experiments, we varied the duration between the final frame of the morph sequence and the onset of the probe (Experiment 2a, 1000 ms; Experiment 2b, 333 ms).
Studies outside of emotion perception suggest that the largest predictive influences on motion perception are at about 300 ms after stimulus presentation (e.g., Hubbard, 2005; Zucchini et al., 2023).

text.text: However, these timings usually reflect influences of lower-order expectations derived directly from the seen motion itself (e.g., a simple extrapolation of prior trajectories).

A recent study suggests that integration of higher-order expectations and sensory information happens at a later stage, when recurrent processing between levels in the hierarchy has taken place (Ntikas et al., 2025, also  see Hogendoorn, 2022).

text.text: Therefore, varying the timing between to-be-judged stimulus and reference image allows us to test whether any predictive influence on emotion perception is immediate, or occurs only after recurrent feedback processes were able to affect the representation of the seen stimulus.

To exclude these participants, we subtracted the average proportion of "different" responses across all probes for congruent Face Emotion and Emotion Statement conditions from the proportion of "different" responses for incongruent Face Emotion and Emotion Statement conditions.

High positive values, therefore, indicate that participants judged congruent Face Emotion and Emotion Statement combinations as "same" more than incongruent pairings, regardless of the dissimilarity of the probe.

Positive values indicate that more expressive probe faces were more likely to be judged as the "same" as the final facial morph expression, suggesting emotion overestimation, while negative values indicate underestimation.
We first tested whether dynamic facial expressions were generally overestimated, so that more expressive probes were more likely to be judged as "same" than less expressive probes.
To do so, we tested average overestimation scores across conditions against zero.

Indeed, overestimation values were consistently positive, showing a general overestimation of facial expressions in both Experiment 2a, t(99) = 5.625, p < .001, d = .56, 95% CI [.35, .77] and Experiment 2b, t(99) = 13.789, p < .001, d = 1.38, 95% CI [1.10, 1.65] (Figure 3A, 3B).

The overestimation scores were therefore analyzed using a 2 (Face Emotion) x 2 (Emotion Statement) repeated measures ANOVA.

We then explored whether this interaction was present in the first half of Experiment 2b (108 trials), as participants may have habituated to the statements across the experiment, reducing their effect.
As the expression representation should be highly precise especially during short delays, this could further limit any influence of prior expectations on emotion perception in Experiment 2b.

While prior information indeed modulated the extent of overestimation in the first half of the trials in Experiment 2b (p = .01) but not in the second half of trials (p = .46, see supplemental materials), a preregistered replication could not confirm this (see Supplementary Experiment 1).
Prior information about someone's emotional state therefore affects the perceptual representation of their expression after 1000ms but we found little evidence for this at 333ms.
Experiments 2a and 2b confirmed that perceptual representations of dynamic facial expressions are biased away from what was objectively presented, and towards expectations.
Facial expressions were generally overestimated, so that participants identified a more expressive probe face to be identical to the last seen expression.
This is in line with the proposal that perception of dynamic facial expression is shaped by expectations of how the expressions will develop further (e.g., Yoshikawa & Sato, 2008).

text.text: Importantly, it showed for the first time that prior information about how the person is feeling determines this overestimation.

We found stronger overestimation when participants expected the current facial expression based on the information that they had received about the person's emotional state, compared to when they expected a different facial expression.

Interestingly, this was the case only when there was longer time (1000ms, Experiment 2a) between the final face that participants saw and the probe face they judged it against, and not for shorter intervals (333ms, Experiment 2b).

One limitation of Experiments 2a and 2b is that they relied upon a highly artificial experimental situation to demonstrate the influence of prior information, using prototypical and repetitive auditory statements that explicitly stated how a person is feeling ("I feel so happy/sad") and were pronounced in the corresponding emotion.
The preregistered Experiment 3 therefore tested whether the effects replicate with more complex cues, in an experimental setting that more closely reflects everyday interactions.

Before the initial face changed expression, participants were presented with two possible written news statements that could evoke happiness or sadness, one of which they could decide to "give" to the other person.

The face then started changing facial expression and, after it disappeared mid-movement, was followed by a probe face (1000 ms gap), which was more or less expressive than the final morph face (as in Experiment 2a).
Participants judged whether the probe face was "same"/"different" to the final expression they had seen.

If the influence of prior information generalizes to a more ecological experimental situation, facial expressions should again be overestimated, and this overestimation should depend on whether the participants expected this emotional response or a different one.

The use of written, rather than auditory statements, also allows us to disentangle whether any such effects are driven by the emotional vocalization or, as hypothesized, by expectations about the person's emotional state and the facial expressions through which this state should manifest itself.

Given a one-sided test with alpha of .05, power of 80%, four looks, and the O'Brien-Fleming type alpha and beta spending functions, maximally 181 participants would be needed, after exclusions.
The four preregistered looks were at 40% (N = 73), 50% (N = 91), 75% (N = 136), and 100% of the data (N = 181).

Alpha boundaries for these looks were p = .002 (look 1), p = .005 (look 2), p = .022 (look 3), and p = .043 (look 4), allowing to stop data collection early when the p-value is smaller than the boundary.

Due to online data collection, we recruited two more participants for look 2 than intended (93 instead of 91) and adjusted the design parameters accordingly.

Twenty happy and twenty sad statements were initially created to reflect news that could be given to a person that is likely to evoke the corresponding emotion in them and were used in Supplementary Experiment 2.

Ten happy statements and ten sad statements, which were rated as the most emotionally intense in a separate experiment (participants were asked, "What intensity of emotion would this news evoke if it was given to a person?"
on a 0-100 scale from "Not intense at all" to "Extremely intense"), were chosen for this experiment.
Example statements were "It seems like your phone call probably saved his life" (happy) or "I got a call from the vet.

The procedure was similar to Experiment 2a (see Figure 3.1).

text.text: On each trial, after the fixation cross (1000 ms), an initial facial expression appeared in the middle of the screen, which was followed 49 frames later (e.g., for 60hz refresh rate display, approximately 817 ms) by one happy and one sad statement presented on the left and right side of the face, position randomized.
The experiment was set up so that participants gave an equal number of happy and sad news over its course (108 each).

Participants could freely choose the statement they wanted to give, but after each break, they were encouraged to focus on giving more happy or sad news to ensure each was chosen roughly equally towards the end of the experiment.

When participants reached the maximum of statements of one emotion category, in the subsequent trials they were still presented with happy and sad news but were only able to select the less chosen category.
After picking the news, by clicking on the chosen statement, 500 ms later the face started changing expression in 3, 4, or 5 frames, with each frame presented for 83 ms.

After the face disappeared, a probe face was presented 1000 ms later, as in Experiment 2a, and participants decided with a press of a button ("s" vs "d") whether it was the same as or different to the last expression in the sequence.
Participants completed 10 practice trials and 216 experimental trials across six blocks.
Blocks were separated by a 30s break, which participants were able to extend as needed.
We included 22 additional catch trials across the experiment (additional 1 catch trial in practice blocks).

Catch trials looked like a regular trial where participants gave news, however, after choosing the news, participants were presented with the chosen statement and a corresponding "incorrect" statement and had to select which one they had chosen (e.g., "I got a call from your mom.

The current series of experiments tested for the first time a crucial hypothesis of predictive processing accounts of (social) cognition (e.g., Bach & Schenke, 2017; Barrett, 2017; Clark, 2013; Hohwy, 2013; Otten et al., 2017): that prior information about someone's emotional state should not only affect how their emotional expressions are interpreted, but also how the expressions themselves are perceptually represented.

text.text: The results consistently revealed the predicted shaping of face emotion perception by prior information, across tasks and measurement methodologies.

Experiments 1a and 1b showed that prior information about someone's emotional state affected explicit ratings of their facial expression, showing increased ratings of happiness and sadness (Experiment 1a), as well as increased perceived intensity (Experiment 1b) of faces that were congruent with the prior emotion information about the other person.
Thus, the same happy expression was rated as happier (and more intense) when perceivers heard that the person is happy and as sadder (and less intense) when the auditory cue indicated sadness.

This shows, in line with predictive processing proposals (e.g., Clark, 2013; Otten et al., 2017), that face emotion perception integrates prior higher-order information about someone's emotional state with the actual sensory information from the facial expressions.

text.text: Experiments 2a and 2b used a psychophysical task to test for the first time whether prior emotion information does not only affect the evaluation of emotional expressions, like in Experiments 1a and 1b, but also their perceptual representation.
Participants judged whether a (more or less expressive) probe face, presented directly after the dynamic expression, was identical to the final expression in the morph sequence.
We found, first, that dynamic expressions were consistently overestimated, with the final expression judged as more expressive than it actually was.

This finding is in line with prior work suggesting that the perceptual representation of dynamic stimuli is not veridical but biased towards their expected next steps, both within (e.g., Yoshikawa & Sato, 2008) and outside face emotion perception (e.g., Currie et al., 2025; Freyd & Finke, 1984; Hudson, Nicholson, Ellis, & Bach, 2016; Hudson, Nicholson, Simpson et al. 2016; for a review, see Hogendoorn, 2022).
text.formatted: This finding is in line with prior work suggesting that the perceptual representation of dynamic stimuli is not veridical but biased towards their expected next steps, both within (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Yoshikawa & Sato, 2008)</ref> and outside face emotion perception (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Currie et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Freyd & Finke, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Hudson, Nicholson, Ellis, & Bach, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Hudson, Nicholson, Simpson et al. 2016</ref>; for a review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Hogendoorn, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, we found that prior information about how a person is feeling determined these overestimations.

With a sufficient delay (1000 ms) between the final face and probe face in Experiment 2a (but not with a shorter delay in Experiment 2b), participants overestimated facial expressions more when they were preceded by an auditory emotion statement that was congruent with the facial expression change than when it was incongruent, revealing an influence of prior information on the perceptual expectations that shape how other people's emotional expressions are represented.

Finally, Experiment 3 demonstrated that the perceptual shaping through prior information generalizes to a more ecological task, in which participants themselves decided which piece of news to give to another person, and therefore, which emotional state to induce.

Moreover, instead of the stereotypical "I feel so happy/sad" statements of the previous experiments, the statements never mentioned any emotion directly, were provided as written statements without emotional intonation, and captured a wide range of emotional information encountered in everyday life.
Despite these changes, we found similar overestimation of facial expressions, which was again larger when the facial expression change matched the person's expected emotional state.

Greater overestimation of congruent face and news statements, therefore, likely reflects an inferential process where perceivers derive how a situation would make a person feel, which then shapes the perception of the upcoming facial reaction.

Together, the current results show for the first time that prior expectations do not impact only face emotion evaluations but can also shape their perceptual representation, shifting the typical overestimation of dynamic facial expression towards the emotion expected from the person's emotion or news statements.

They challenge basic emotion accounts (e.g., Ekman & Cordaro, 2011), according to which emotions are primarily inferred from facial expressions or other expressor-related perceptual cues, like vocalizations and body language (Keltner, Sauter, et al., 2019; Keltner, Tracy, et al., 2019).
text.formatted: They challenge basic emotion accounts (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Ekman & Cordaro, 2011)</ref>, according to which emotions are primarily inferred from facial expressions or other expressor-related perceptual cues, like vocalizations and body language <ref type="bibr">(Keltner, Sauter, et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Keltner, Tracy, et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In such accounts, prior information only affects the final interpretation of an emotional expression but would not affect the perceptual encoding we observed here.

Instead, our findings support predictive processing accounts (e.g., Barrett, 2017; Clark, 2013) that conceptualize emotion perception, and social perception more generally, as a process of "hypothesis" testing and updating where the final percept reflects an approximate Bayesian integration of top-down expectations and bottom-up sensory input.
text.formatted: Instead, our findings support predictive processing accounts (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Barrett, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Clark, 2013)</ref> that conceptualize emotion perception, and social perception more generally, as a process of "hypothesis" testing and updating where the final percept reflects an approximate Bayesian integration of top-down expectations and bottom-up sensory input.

text.text: In these frameworks, any higher-order interpretational change of facial emotion directly feeds into the perceptual representation of the expression itself, shifting it subtly from what was perceived towards what was expected.

The result is a coherent percept that integrates all available sources of information, so that what one perceives shapes one's higher-order evaluations, and higherorder information, in turn, shapes how expressions are perceptually represented.

Moreover, like we found here, this should happen irrespective of whether the prior expectation comes from the expressor themselves (Experiment 1a to 2b) or from expressor-external information about the emotional situation they are in (Experiment 3).
The current studies provide a substantial methodological advance over prior work.

A problem with previous literature on context effects in face emotion perception is that most studies asked participants to categorize or rate the specific emotions in the facial expressions relative to pre-given emotion labels.

This made it difficult to rule out potential response biases (e.g., Firestone & Scholl, 2016), as it has long been known that available response options directly affect how emotions are categorized (Russell, 1993).
text.formatted: This made it difficult to rule out potential response biases (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Firestone & Scholl, 2016)</ref>, as it has long been known that available response options directly affect how emotions are categorized <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Russell, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: The results may therefore reflect an influence on the rating (or categorization) response itself, biasing them towards sadness or happiness without affecting face emotion evaluation per se.

Experiment 1b for the first time eliminated the mapping between the emotional context and the response options by removing any emotion labels from the ratings, merely asking participants to rate the intensity of the expression, irrespective of the emotion it displayed.

The replication of the influence of prior information on face evaluation with similar effect sizes (emotion ratings, d = .457; intensity ratings, d = .473) substantially limits the potential influences of such response biases.
Experiments 2a, 2b, and 3 further confirmed this.
Here, participants were never asked to judge the emotion in the expression, merely to perceptually compare whether one expression was identical to a probe face presented after.
Nevertheless, a similar shaping of face perception through prior emotion information was observed.

Thus, next to identifying an influence of prior information on the perceptual encoding of facial expressions, these studies provide additional evidence against a role of response biases in producing the resulting changes in either evaluation or subjective perceptual judgements of facial expressions.

The pattern of results across Experiments 2a, 2b, and 3 provides novel insights into the stage of processing in which the integration of prior and perceptual information occurs during face emotion perception.

We found that the general overestimation of facial expressionshappy expressions seen as happier than they really were, sad expressions as sadder -was observed both with short (333 ms, Experiment 2b) and longer (1000 ms, Experiment 2a, Experiment 3) delays between face encoding and probe judgment.
This suggests that lowerorder visual expectations about how a facial expression will develop are integrated rapidly into dynamic face perception.
In contrast, the shaping of these overestimations towards the person's (higher-order) emotional state by predictive cues was restricted to longer delays.
These findings challenge proposals that top-down information may affect even the earliest stages of perceptual processing when retinal input reaches the visual cortex (e.g., Rauss et al., 2011).
text.formatted: These findings challenge proposals that top-down information may affect even the earliest stages of perceptual processing when retinal input reaches the visual cortex (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Rauss et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Instead, it is consistent with recent proposals, which suggest that when perceiving dynamic stimuli, the brain integrates sensory information with prior information from other sources only in a later "editing" stage.

Here, initial stimulus representations are refined and updated, producing a coherent percept that serves as basis for (conscious) perception, decision-making, and action (Hogendoorn, 2022; Schmitt & de Lange, 2025; White, 2026).

text.text: An interesting observation was that, in Experiments 2a and 2b, happy facial expressions were overestimated more than sad facial expressions.
While not predicted, this finding is fully in line with the idea that the observed overestimations reflect the expectations that people have about how the observed motion will develop further.

If so, one would expect reduced overestimation for expressions that already seem to have reached their ultimate state than those further away from it (for an example outside emotion perception, see Hubbard & Motes, 2005).

text.text: Consistent with this hypothesis, Experiment 1b shows that happy facial expressions were indeed rated as less intense than their sad counterparts, as is the case more generally for happy faces in the IASLab face set.
Moreover, the happy facial expressions we used had a closed mouth, which may be perceived as less intense than expressions showing an open-mouth smile.

The increased overestimation for happy expression here is, therefore, fully in line with predictive proposals, in which people expect already intense sad expressions to not develop much further, compared to less intense happy expressions.
The current findings have important implications for our understanding of emotion perception in everyday life.

The ability to predict emotional reactions, such as how people's emotional states transition, is associated with social benefits for the perceiver, such as lower reports of loneliness and larger social networks (Barrick et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2022).

text.text: Since these studies focus on reasoning about other people's hypothetical emotional states, rather than visual perception of changing facial expressions, a promising avenue would be to investigate whether these forms of predictions are related and whether greater overestimation of facial expressions found in our tasks has similar links to social functioning outcomes.

text.text: They highlight the importance of including contextual cues in experimental paradigms to provide a fuller picture of how emotions are inferred and perceived from the face, as well as in computational models designed to capture human emotion perception in the field of computer vision and machine learning.

The present study provides a systematic investigation of how expectations impact dynamic emotion perception, showing that both emotion evaluation and perception can be affected by prior information about someone's emotion state, as measured across different response tasks and different types of cues.
However, there are some important limitations and constraints on generality to consider when interpreting these findings.
First, to increase the experimental control of the facial movement, we relied upon dynamic facial morphs, which have been widely used to study dynamic emotion perception (Dobs et al., 2018).

text.text: However, naturalistic spontaneous dynamic expressions may be more ambiguous than the linearly morphed expressions relied upon here, as the former may better capture important temporal features of muscle movements, such as the movement onset, acceleration, and offset, increasing the variability in sensory evidence.

Interestingly, predictive processing proposals assume that contextual influences should be, if anything, enhanced for such ambiguous expressions, as less precise perceptual representations provide fewer constraints on top-down influences and, therefore, are weighted less in the integration process (e.g., Yon & Frith, 2021; Pullinen et al., 2026).

text.text: In both cases, larger effects of prior emotion information than those observed here would be expected.
Second, our studies focused on understanding how prior information is relied upon in face emotion perception in young and middle-aged adults (range across experiments was 18-49 years old).

Research comparing context reliance between younger and older adults in face emotion judgements does suggest age-related differences, with older people relying more on context compared to younger adults (e.g., Noh & Isaacowitz, 2013; Lawrie et al., 2025; in these studies, older adults were 59/60+, younger were 17-29).

text.text: Our experimental paradigm could, therefore, be used in future research to investigate whether the effects found in the present studies become even more pronounced with age.

Furthermore, while parts of our studies relied mostly on the student population (e.g., Experiment 1a), experiments that relied solely or partially on data collection through online participation platforms (e.g., Experiment 1b, 3) potentially have recruited a more diverse group of participants, although no individual differences information (e.g., ethnicity) has been collected to confirm this.

The present studies have, however, recruited participants residing in English-speaking countries, to ensure spontaneous processing of the emotion cues, with a large part of the sample including participants from the UK.

Therefore, this limits our understanding as to what type of information is important when making face emotion judgements and how people's expectations of the likely emotion may differ across different cultures, especially in the context of Experiment 3 that included statements that required a situation-to-emotion inference.

When judging how a person is feeling from their facial expressions, perceivers use different sources of information to inform their judgements, as reflected in findings of context effects in face evaluation.
Predictive processing accounts propose that these effects reflect participants' expectations shaping not only face emotion evaluation but also the perceptual representation of facial expressions.

We tested this across five experiments and found for the first time that these expectations shape not only explicit face evaluation but also the perceptual representation of dynamic facial expressions at a later stage of face emotion processing.

These findings are in line with recent predictive processing accounts, which propose that perceivers rely on various sources of information to predict the upcoming facial expression, leading to differences in how these expressions are represented.
